title: First steps in poetry: reading a classical poem
intro: Iranians quote poetry the way other people quote proverbs, and almost all of it is classical. In this lesson you learn how a classical poem is put together – the بیت and its two halves, the rhyme and the refrain, the poet's pen name – how to hear the rhythm by counting long and short syllables, and the old short forms that poets use. Then you read Saadi's بنی‌آدم line by line and find out how Iranians ask Hafez about their future on Yalda night.
goals: name the parts of a poem: بیت، مصراع، قافیه، ردیف، تخلص
tell a غزل from a رباعی، a مثنوی and a قصیده
hear the metre by counting long and short syllables
recognise the poetic forms ز، چو، همی، -ا، دگر، کز and give their modern equivalents
read Saadi's بنی‌آدم line by line and explain fāl-e Hāfez

sections.title: Children of Adam
sections.intro: Saadi of Shiraz finished his *Golestan* ('The Rose Garden') in 1258. Here is the story behind its most famous lines, and the three bayts themselves, each followed by a plain modern version that begins with یعنی 'that is'. Watch for the short forms ز، چو، دگر and کز.

sentences.r: Sa'di, shā'er-e bozorg-e Shirāz, hodud-e hashtsad sāl pish zendegi mi-kard.
sentences.en: Saadi, the great poet of Shiraz, lived about eight hundred years ago.
sentences.faV: سَعدی، شاعِرِ بُزُرگِ شیراز، حُدودِ هَشتصَد سال پیش زِندِگی می‌کَرد.

sentences.r: pādeshāh az Sa'di khāst ke barā-yash do'ā konad.
sentences.en: The king asked Saadi to pray for him.

sentences.fa: سعدی به او گفت که به مردم ضعیف رحم کند و این سه بیت را خواند.
sentences.r: Sa'di be u goft ke be mardom-e za'if rahm konad va in se beyt rā khānd.
sentences.en: Saadi told him to have mercy on the weak, and recited these three bayts.

sentences.fa: بنی‌آدم اعضای یکدیگرند / که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند
sentences.r: bani-ādam a'zā-ye yekdigar-and / ke dar āfarinesh ze yek gowhar-and
sentences.en: The children of Adam are limbs of one another, / for in creation they are made of one essence.
sentences.note: [[ز|ze]] = [[از|az]]; [[یکدیگرند|yekdigar-and]] = [[یکدیگر هستند|yekdigar hastand]]. Many people quote the first half as «بنی‌آدم اعضای یک پیکرند» – 'limbs of one body'.

sentences.fa: یعنی همه‌ی انسان‌ها اعضای یک بدن هستند، چون از یک اصل آفریده شده‌اند.
sentences.r: ya'ni hame-ye ensān-hā a'zā-ye yek badan hastand, chon az yek asl āfaride shode-and.
sentences.en: In other words, all human beings are limbs of one body, because they were created from one origin.
sentences.faV: یَعنی هَمه‌یِ اِنسان‌ها اَعضایِ یِک بَدَن هَستَند، چون اَز یِک اَصل آفَریده شُده‌اَند.

sentences.fa: چو عضوی به درد آورد روزگار / دگر عضوها را نماند قرار
sentences.r: cho 'ozvi be dard āvarad ruzgār / degar 'ozv-hā rā namānad gharār
sentences.en: When the world brings pain to one limb, / the other limbs can find no rest.
sentences.note: [[چو|cho]] = [[وقتی که|vaghti ke]]; [[دگر|degar]] = [[دیگر|digar]]; [[عضوها را|'ozv-hā rā]] = 'for the limbs'. The verbs [[آورد|āvarad]] and [[نماند|namānad]] have no می: this is always true.
sentences.faV: چو عُضوی به دَرد آوَرَد روزگار / دِگَر عُضوها را نَمانَد قَرار

sentences.fa: یعنی وقتی یک عضو بدن درد می‌کشد، عضوهای دیگر هم آرام نمی‌گیرند.
sentences.r: ya'ni vaghti yek 'ozv-e badan dard mi-keshad, 'ozv-hā-ye digar ham ārām nemi-girand.
sentences.en: In other words, when one limb of the body hurts, the other limbs cannot rest either.
sentences.faV: یَعنی وَقتی یِک عُضوِ بَدَن دَرد می‌کِشَد، عُضوهایِ دیگَر هَم آرام نِمی‌گیرَند.

sentences.fa: تو کز محنت دیگران بی‌غمی / نشاید که نامت نهند آدمی
sentences.r: to kaz mehnat-e digarān bi-ghami / nashāyad ke nām-at nahand ādami
sentences.en: You who feel no grief at the suffering of others / do not deserve to be called human.
sentences.lit: you who from the suffering of others are without-sorrow, it is not fitting that they put your name 'human'
sentences.note: [[کز|kaz]] = [[که از|ke az]]; [[نشاید|nashāyad]] = 'it is not fitting' (from the old verb شایستن); [[نهند|nahand]] = 'they put' (نهادن = گذاشتن).
sentences.faV: تو کَز مِحنَتِ دیگَران بی‌غَمی / نَشایَد که نامَت نَهَند آدَمی

sentences.fa: یعنی اگر از رنج دیگران غمگین نمی‌شوی، شایسته نیست که تو را انسان بنامند.
sentences.r: ya'ni agar az ranj-e digarān ghamgin nemi-shavi, shāyeste nist ke to rā ensān benāmand.
sentences.en: In other words, if the suffering of others does not sadden you, you do not deserve to be called human.
sentences.faV: یَعنی اَگَر اَز رَنجِ دیگَران غَمگین نِمی‌شَوی، شایِسته نیست که تو را اِنسان بِنامَند.

sentences.fa: امروز بچه‌های ایرانی این شعر را در مدرسه از بر می‌کنند.
sentences.r: emruz bacche-hā-ye irāni in she'r rā dar madrese az bar mi-konand.
sentences.en: Today Iranian children learn this poem by heart at school.
sentences.faV: اِمروز بَچّه‌هایِ ایرانی این شِعر را دَر مَدرِسه اَز بَر می‌کُنَند.

sentences.r: ba'd az har zelzele yā seyl, mardom beyt-e avval-e ān rā dar payām-hā-yeshān mi-nevisand.
sentences.en: After every earthquake or flood, people write its first bayt in their messages.

sections.title: How to read a bayt
sections.md:
Iranians quote poetry the way English speakers quote proverbs – at weddings and funerals, in arguments, in text messages – and almost all of it is **classical**, written between the 10th and the 15th centuries. Persian has changed so little since then that a schoolchild in Tehran can read Saadi. What makes old poems hard is not so much the words as the way they are put together.

A classical poem is a chain of [[بیت|beyt|bayts]]: lines in two halves. Each half is a [[مصراع|mesrā']]. Books print the two halves side by side – read the **right-hand half first**, then the left – and in this course they are separated by ` / `.

Four things will surprise you after modern prose:

1. **Free word order.** To fit the rhythm, a verb can come before its subject: [[چو عضوی به درد آورد روزگار|cho 'ozvi be dard āvarad ruzgār]] is literally *when a limb to pain brings – the world*.
2. **Short forms.** [[ز|ze]] for [[از|az]], [[چو|cho]] for [[چون|chon]], [[دگر|degar]] for [[دیگر|digar]]: a syllable shorter, to fit the metre.
3. **No می.** The bare present [[آورد|āvarad]] means *brings – always brings*: a general truth.
4. **Arabic.** Poets mixed in Arabic words and sometimes whole Arabic half-lines; Hafez's very first line begins in Arabic.

The good news: the world of the poems is small. The same cupbearer, wine, garden, nightingale and cruel beloved come back again and again, so every poem you read makes the next one easier.

sections.title: The anatomy of a poem: bayt, rhyme, refrain – and the four forms
sections.md:
Every classical poem is built from the same parts.

The **rhyme**, [[قافیه|ghāfiye]], is the sound that comes back at the end of the lines. After it there may be a **refrain**, [[ردیف|radif]]: one or more words repeated, unchanged, at the end of every rhyming line. A rhyme is compulsory; a radif is a choice – and the great poets love it, because it makes every bayt land on the same words.

- In Hafez's first ghazal the rhyme is *-el* and the radif is only [[ها|-hā]]: nāv**el-hā**, moshk**el-hā**, d**el-hā**, manz**el-hā**, sāh**el-hā**, mahf**el-hā**…
- In his ghazal of Joseph the radif is a whole phrase, [[غم مخور|gham ma-khor|do not grieve]], and the rhyme is the word just before it: Kan'**ān**, golest**ān**…
- Saadi's بنی‌آدم has rhymes but no radif – and each of its bayts rhymes on its own, like a small masnavi.

In a **ghazal** both halves of the first bayt rhyme; after that only the second half of each bayt does: *aa ba ca da…* The last bayt usually names the poet by his pen name, the [[تخلص|takhallos]]: Hafez and Saadi often speak to themselves in their last lines. The other forms differ in length and in how they rhyme:

examples.r: hozur-i gar hami-khāhi az u ghāyeb ma-show Hāfez
examples.en: If you want to be in His presence, do not be absent from Him, Hafez.

examples.faV: حُضوری گَر هَمی‌خواهی اَز او غایِب مَشَو حافِظ

examples.r: Yusef-e gom-gashte bāz āyad be Kan'ān gham ma-khor / kolbe-ye ahzān shavad ruz-i golestān gham ma-khor
examples.en: Lost Joseph will come back to Canaan – do not grieve; / the hut of sorrows will one day be a rose garden – do not grieve.
examples.note: Hafez again. Radif: [[غم مخور|gham ma-khor]]; rhyme: [[کنعان|Kan'ān]] / [[گلستان|golestān]]. The 'hut of sorrows' is where Jacob mourned his lost son Joseph until he came home.

examples.fa: این قافله‌ی عمر عجب می‌گذرد / دریاب دمی که با طرب می‌گذرد
examples.r: in ghāfele-ye 'omr 'ajab mi-gozarad / daryāb dam-i ke bā tarab mi-gozarad
examples.en: How strangely this caravan of life goes by! / Seize the moment that passes in joy.
examples.note: A robā'i attributed to Khayyam, first bayt. Rhyme: [[عجب|'ajab]] / [[طرب|tarab]]; radif: [[می‌گذرد|mi-gozarad]].
examples.faV: این قافِله‌یِ عُمر عَجَب می‌گُذَرَد / دَریاب دَمی که با طَرَب می‌گُذَرَد

examples.r: sāghi gham-e fardā-ye harifān che khori / pish ār piyāle rā ke shab mi-gozarad
examples.en: Cupbearer, why grieve over your companions' tomorrow? / Bring the cup, for the night is passing.
examples.note: The second bayt: the third line does not rhyme, the fourth comes back to [[شب|shab]] + [[می‌گذرد|mi-gozarad]] – the pattern aa ba.
examples.faV: ساقی غَمِ فَردایِ حَریفان چه خوری / پیش آر پیاله را که شَب می‌گُذَرَد

examples.fa: بشنو این نی چون شکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها حکایت می‌کند
examples.r: beshnow in ney chon shekāyat mi-konad / az jodāyi-hā hekāyat mi-konad
examples.en: Listen to this reed, how it complains, / telling the tale of separations.
examples.note: The first bayt of Rumi's Masnavi, which runs to over 25,000 bayts, each rhyming on its own: here [[شکایت|shekāyat]] / [[حکایت|hekāyat]] with the radif [[می‌کند|mi-konad]]. Often quoted as «بشنو از نی چون حکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها شکایت می‌کند».

examples.fa: بوی جوی مولیان آید همی / یاد یار مهربان آید همی
examples.r: bu-ye ju-ye Muliyān āyad hami / yād-e yār-e mehrabān āyad hami
examples.en: The scent of the Muliyan stream comes to me, / the memory of a dear friend comes to me.
examples.note: The opening of a qasida by Rudaki (died 941), the first great poet of Persian. The Samanid emir had stayed too long in Herat; when Rudaki sang this, the story goes, he jumped on his horse without his boots and rode home to Bukhara. Radif: [[آید همی|āyad hami]]; rhyme: [[مولیان|Muliyān]] / [[مهربان|mehrabān]].

sections.title: Long and short: hearing the metre
sections.md:
Classical verse has a strict rhythm, its [[وزن|vazn|metre]]: a fixed pattern of long and short syllables, [[هجا|hejā]]. You don't need the technical names to hear it – just two rules:

- **Short** (∪): a consonant + a short vowel *a, e, o* that ends the syllable: *ba, ke, ze, ye*.
- **Long** (–): a long vowel *ā, i, u* or *ow, ey* – *ni, ā, gow* – or any vowel closed by a consonant: *dar, yek, nesh*.

Two more facts make it work. Words **run together** across the space, so *ādam a'zā* is read *ā-da-ma'-zā*. And the last syllable of a mesrā' always counts as long.

Saadi's lines are in the metre called [[متقارب|motaghāreb]], the metre of Ferdowsi's *Shahnameh*: three groups of ∪ – – and a short ∪ –, *da-DUM-DUM da-DUM-DUM da-DUM-DUM da-DUM*. Hafez's first ghazal is in [[هزج|hazaj]], four groups of ∪ – – –. Rumi's *Masnavi* is in [[رمل|ramal]]: – ∪ – –, – ∪ – –, – ∪ –. Tap the long syllables as you read aloud and you will hear the difference.

examples.note: *ke-'esh-ghā-sān / ne-mu-dav-val / va-li-of-tā / d-mosh-kel-hā*. The syllable *tād* (a long vowel + a consonant) counts as long + short: its *d* is the short beat that opens the last group.

examples.en: Listen to this reed, how it complains, / telling the tale of separations.
examples.note: *besh-no-vin-ney / chon-she-kā-yat / mi-ko-nad*: – ∪ – –, – ∪ – –, – ∪ –. The *ow* of *beshnow* becomes *o-v* before the vowel of *in*.

sections.title: The poet's short forms: ز، چو، همی، -ا، دگر، کز
sections.md:
Poets needed words that were a syllable shorter or longer, so poetry kept old and short forms that modern prose has dropped. Learn them once and you can read a thousand years of verse – and many proverbs, which are often lines of poetry.

Most are simply **short forms**: [[ز|ze]] is [[از|az]], [[دگر|degar]] is [[دیگر|digar]], [[گر|gar]] is [[اگر|agar]]. Some are **two words run together**: [[کز|kaz]] = [[که از|ke az]], [[کاین|kin]] = [[که این|ke in]], [[زان|zān]] = [[از آن|az ān]].

The **-ā** at the end of a word has two jobs. On a person it calls them: [[ساقیا|sāghiyā|O cupbearer!]], [[حافظا|Hāfezā|O Hafez!]], [[خدایا|khodāyā|O God!]] – the last one is still everyday Persian. On a few words it means *how much!*: [[بسا|basā|many a…]] (from [[بس|bas|much]]), which lives on in [[چه بسا|che basā|quite possibly]].

[[همی|hami]] is the old form of [[می‌|mi-]], and in early poems it can even stand after the verb: [[آید همی|āyad hami]] = [[می‌آید|mi-āyad|keeps coming]]. Very often there is no prefix at all: the bare present [[آورد|āvarad]] = [[می‌آورد|mi-āvarad]], used for what is always true.

sections.title: A fortune from Hafez
sections.context: It is Yalda night at Leila's family home. Tom saw a Hafez fortune taken last year but did not understand a word, so Leila explains – and then takes one for him.

lines.fa: لیلا، پارسال در خانه‌ی پدربزرگ مینا فال حافظ گرفتیم، ولی من چیزی از شعرش نفهمیدم.
lines.r: Leylā, pārsāl dar khāne-ye pedar-bozorg-e Minā fāl-e Hāfez gereftim, vali man chiz-i az she'r-ash na-fahmidam.
lines.en: Leila, last year we took a Hafez fortune at Mina's grandfather's house, but I didn't understand anything of the poem.
lines.col: لیلا، پارسال خونه‌ی پدربزرگ مینا فال حافظ گرفتیم، ولی من هیچی از شعرش نفهمیدم.
lines.colR: Leylā, pārsāl khune-ye pedar-bozorg-e Minā fāl-e Hāfez gereftim, vali man hichi az she'r-esh na-fahmidam.

lines.en: No – before that you say: 'O Hafez of Shiraz, you who keep every secret – I beg you by your Shakh-e Nabat!'

lines.fa: یوسف گم‌گشته باز آید به کنعان غم مخور / کلبه‌ی احزان شود روزی گلستان غم مخور

sections.title: Hafez in the garden, Hafez in song
sections.md:
**The Hāfeziye.** Hafez died in Shiraz in 1390 and was buried in a garden outside the city. His tomb, the [[حافظیه|Hāfeziye]], is an open pavilion of eight columns under a dome tiled on the inside, among orange trees – less a monument than a meeting place. Visitors lay a hand on the carved stone and murmur a ghazal, students come at sunset, couples come on dates, and fortune-sellers at the gate offer a folded verse, sometimes picked out of a box by a canary. On [[۲۰ مهر|bistom-e Mehr]] (12 October), the Day of Hafez, the garden is full of readers; Saadi has his own day on [[۱ اردیبهشت|avval-e Ordibehesht]] (21 April), at his own tomb a few kilometres away.

**Poetry you can hear.** The word [[ردیف|radif]] has a second life: it is also the name of the traditional repertoire of Persian classical music, the melodies that masters pass on to their students by ear. Singers of [[آواز|āvāz]] choose a ghazal by Hafez, Saadi or Rumi and stretch it over the melody, long syllables long and short ones short, exactly where the metre puts them. Many Iranians first learn the great ghazals from songs – one reason they feel the metre without ever studying it.

**By heart.** Children learn poems [[از بر|az bar|by heart]] at school, and many adults can recite dozens of ghazals. Quote a well-chosen bayt at the right moment and an Iranian friend will often answer with another.

sections.title: Tips
items: Read the right-hand mesrā' first, then the left. In books the two halves stand side by side; online they are often on two lines or separated by a slash.
Find the verb first – it may be anywhere in the line – then the subject, then put the line into modern prose order in your head: چو عضوی به درد آورد روزگار → وقتی روزگار عضوی را به درد می‌آورد.
When you meet ز، چو، کز، دگر، گر، همی, say the modern form silently: از، چون، که از، دیگر، اگر، می. After a few poems you will stop noticing them.
Read aloud. If the rhythm limps, you have probably misread a vowel: the metre tells you where an ezafe goes and where it does not.
A long vowel + a consonant (tād, ruz) or a short vowel + two consonants (dard, 'ozv) counts as long + short – a beat and a half. That is how lines that look too short still fill the pattern.
Learn one bayt a week by heart. Quoting Saadi or Hafez at the right moment is the warmest compliment you can pay the language – and Iranians will notice.

The other limbs do not stay calm.

items.fa: ___ حضور می‌خواهی، از او غایب نشو.
items.r: ___ hozur mi-khāhi, az u ghāyeb na-show.
items.en: If you want to be with him, don't be absent from him.
The scent of the Muliyan stream keeps coming.

items.q: What do you call one half of a bayt?
items.explain: Every bayt has two مصراع; books print them side by side.

items.q: In [[یوسف گم‌گشته باز آید به کنعان غم مخور|Yusef-e gom-gashte bāz āyad be Kan'ān gham ma-khor]], which words are the radif?
items.explain: The radif comes back unchanged at the end of every bayt, after the rhyme word (کنعان، گلستان…).

items.q: Which form has four mesrā's rhyming aa ba?
items.explain: The robā'i (from the Arabic for 'fourfold') – Khayyam's form.

items.q: Ferdowsi told the story of Iran's kings and heroes in some 50,000 bayts. Which form did he use?
items.explain: In a masnavi every bayt has its own rhyme, so the poet never runs out of rhyming words, however long the story.

items.q: Is the first syllable of [[بنی‌آدم|bani-ādam]] long or short?
items.explain: ba is a consonant + the short vowel a with nothing after it: short. The next syllable, ni, has a long i: long.

items.q: In a ghazal by Saadi, which word would you expect to find in the last bayt?
items.explain: The last bayt usually carries the poet's takhallos – his own pen name.

items.fa: حافظ در قرن چهاردهم میلادی در شیراز زندگی می‌کرد.
items.r: Hāfez dar gharn-e chahārdahom-e milādi dar Shirāz zendegi mi-kard.
items.en: Hafez lived in Shiraz in the fourteenth century AD.
items.faV: حافِظ دَر قَرنِ چَهاردَهُمِ میلادی دَر شیراز زِندِگی می‌کَرد.

items.fa: هر بیت از دو مصراع ساخته شده است.
items.r: har beyt az do mesrā' sākhte shode ast.
items.en: Every bayt is made of two mesrā's.
items.faV: هَر بَیت اَز دو مِصراع ساخته شُده اَست.

items.en: The radif comes after the rhyme.

items.fa: بچه‌ها این شعر را در مدرسه از بر می‌کنند.
items.r: bacche-hā in she'r rā dar madrese az bar mi-konand.
items.en: Children learn this poem by heart at school.
items.faV: بَچّه‌ها این شِعر را دَر مَدرِسه اَز بَر می‌کُنَند.

items.en: Saadi is one of the greatest poets of the Persian language.
items.fa: سعدی یکی از بزرگ‌ترین شاعران زبان فارسی است.
items.r: Sa'di yek-i az bozorg-tarin shā'erān-e zabān-e fārsi ast.
items.faV: سَعدی یِکی اَز بُزُرگ‌تَرین شاعِرانِ زَبانِ فارسی اَست.

items.en: The last bayt of a ghazal contains the poet's pen name.
items.fa: بیت آخر غزل تخلص شاعر را دارد.
items.r: beyt-e ākhar-e ghazal takhallos-e shā'er rā dārad.
items.faV: بَیتِ آخَرِ غَزَل تَخَلُّصِ شاعِر را دارَد.

items.en: Make a wish, then open the Divan.
items.fa: نیت کن، بعد دیوان را باز کن.
items.r: niyyat kon, ba'd divān rā bāz kon.
items.faV: نیَّت کُن، بَعد دیوان را باز کُن.

items.en: All human beings are limbs of one body.
items.fa: همه‌ی انسان‌ها اعضای یک بدن هستند.
items.r: hame-ye ensān-hā a'zā-ye yek badan hastand.
items.faV: هَمه‌یِ اِنسان‌ها اَعضایِ یِک بَدَن هَستَند.

items.fa: یوسف گم‌گشته باز آید به کنعان غم مخور
items.r: Yusef-e gom-gashte bāz āyad be Kan'ān gham ma-khor
items.en: Lost Joseph will come back to Canaan – do not grieve.
options: Joseph went to Canaan and was sad.
Lost Joseph will come back to Canaan – do not grieve.
items.faV: یوسِفِ گُم‌گَشته باز آیَد به کَنعان غَم مَخور

items.en: The children of Adam are limbs of one another.
options: The children of Adam are limbs of one another.
Adam's children live far from each other.

items.fa: این غزل را از بر کرده‌ام.
items.r: in ghazal rā az bar karde-am.
items.en: I have learnt this ghazal by heart.
options: I have learnt this ghazal by heart.
items.faV: این غَزَل را اَز بَر کَرده‌اَم.
